title: Did Villar properties benefit from flood control projects?
text: MANILA, Philippines – Who paid for the flood control projects in Las Piñas and Cavite that allegedly benefited some Villar properties? This is what the new Ombudsman task force wants to probe into , according to Ombudsman Boying Remulla. He said the task force will also investigate all government infrastructure projects linked to the Villars. Earlier, a Rappler investigation revealed that Motiontrade — a firm owned by Christian Aguilar (Senator Mark and Camille Villar’s uncle) — bagged P390 million worth of flood control projects. Rappler reporter Jairo Bolledo explains. – Rappler.com Reporter, writer, producer, video editor: Jairo Bolledo Supervising editor: Isagani de Castro How does this make you feel?

title: LIST: Top flood control contractors in Visayas towns where Tino was deadliest
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Who constructed the flood control projects that should have prevented the deaths caused by Typhoon Tino? The deadliest storm to hit the country this year, Tino and the destruction it left in its wake have sparked even more public outrage over the flood control controversy that first erupted earlier in July. Now, people are asking: Who should be held accountable? The government, at both the national and local levels, has pointed to the doubtful quality of flood control projects in the area. Here are the top flood control contractors of provinces where Tino caused the most deaths. Cebu province ranks second for most flood control projects and highest total cost of projects from 2022 to 2025. This is despite not being among the top 10 most flood-prone provinces in the country. But when Tino hit, it showed that the number and cost of these flood control projects did not equate to safety for the province. Scores of people still died, especially in the towns of Liloan, Compostela, Cebu City, Mandaue City, Danao City, Balamban, and Talisay City. So, since 2022, who built the flood control projects in these areas? In Liloan, where Tino claimed the most lives, Discaya -linked firms, in partnership with MC Geometric Proportions Inc., secured the highest total cost of contracts. These projects were supposed to prevent the Cotcot River from overflowing and flooding the surrounding land. But the waters still rose above the river’s banks, submerging the communities living downstream, as shown in a simulation released by the Cebu Provincial Capitol. Province-wide, QM Builders and Quirante Construction took the biggest slice of projects overall. Most of their projects were built to control the Mananga River in Talisay City, but a Sunstar report found that the shanties under and on the sides of the Mananga Bridge were still destroyed by the strong current. QM Builders is owned by Allan Quirante , who famously flip-flopped during a Senate probe into his company’s projects. Quirante Construction is led by Jonathan Quirante, and sources who requested anonymity told Rappler that Jonathan is Allan’s nephew. (READ: Dumanjug’s Quirante clan took nearly 1 of 4 flood control projects in Cebu ) Negros Island is another area where Tino caused grave destruction, especially in Negros Occidental. From 2022 to 2025, ₱9.5 billion-worth of flood control projects were built in the area — though they failed to stop the recent typhoon from claiming several lives in the province. The Camansi and Binalbagan Rivers are located in the towns of La Castellana and Hinigaran, respectively. River control projects supposed to keep these bodies of water at bay were built by the country’s top flood control contractor: Legacy Construction Corporation. The firm is owned by Alex Abelido, who is also a prominent figure in Negros Occidental. Rappler had previously reported on his company’s flood control projects being flooded back in July. (READ: Most Negros Occidental projects of Marcos-listed top contractor flooded in July ) Another report by Rappler in August found that Legacy Construction Corporation had previously received poor and unsatisfactory ratings from the Constructors’ Performance Evaluation System for road widening and drainage projects in 2020. On the other side of the island, Canlaon City in Negros Oriental was also among the hardest hit by Typhoon Tino. Data show that only one flood control project was built in the city from 2022 to 2025: a box culvert along the Vallehermoso-Canlaon City-La Castellana road constructed by Rekina Construction Services. The town had already been grappling with repeated activity from nearby Kanlaon Volcano when the typhoon struck. Before Tino made landfall, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) had already issued a warning for lahar and sediment flows. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

title: Anomalous? Only 2 of 254 flood control works were approved by Quezon City
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. QUEZON CITY. Thick clouds envelop Pasig and Quezon City on June 3, 2025. Jire Carreon/Rappler MANILA, Philippines – Only 2 out of the 254 flood control projects of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in Quezon City were approved by the city government, raising suspicions that some of the flood control works in the Philippines’ richest and largest city may be anomalous. The rest of the flood control projects, worth P14.24 billion, had disapproved, incomplete, or lacking certificates of coordination required under the Local Government Code and the policy of the city government. Only 16 out of the 254 projects tried to apply for a certificate of coordination. “I am convinced that there are anomalous projects,” Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte said in a press briefing on Friday, August 29. “It’s quite suspect for me — I’m talking on a personal basis — that we have all these policies in place that require you to coordinate,” she added. All flood control projects in Quezon City currently under inspection were supposedly constructed from 2021 to 2025. Quezon City said that aside from the certificates of coordination being required by law, they need these in order to align the projects with the city’s drainage master plan, conducted with the University of the Philippines Resilience Institute. According to city engineer Dale Perral, the certificate is a prerequisite for other permits needed for construction. The city government has so far completed the inspection of 93 flood control projects worth P6.64 billion in total. Some of the disapproved projects the local government identified were the Matalahib Creek pumping station (worth P95,998,547), the Mariblo pumping station (worth P282,850,771.95), and the Sta. Cruz pumping station (worth P282,847,634.84). Bypassing the local government is an issue not only in flood control projects but also in other DPWH projects. Of the 1,652 DPWH projects in Quezon City from 2021 to 2025, only 138 or 8.4% have approved certificates of coordination. During Friday’s press briefing, local officials enumerated the following observations from their on-site inspections of flood control works: A particularly anomalous flood control project identified as “Construction of Mendez Creek, Brgy. Baesa, QC” now had a roadway above the creek. According to Carlo Lopez Austria, head of city legal department, there are many legal recourse against violators. “There are actions where we can file administrative as well as criminal charges for violations of the Local Government Code, Water Code, National Building Code, among others,” Austria said in a mix of English and Filipino during the briefing. title: TRACKER: Status of legal actions vs actors in flood control corruption
text:
SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. FILING. Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) 
Chairperson Andres Reyes Jr., along with volunteer lawyers, file cases before the Office of the Ombudsman against Senators Joel Villanueva and Jinggoy Estrada, former Ako Bicol Party list representative Zaldy Co, former Caloocan 2nd District representative Mitch Cajayon-Uy, former DPWH undersecretary Roberto Bernardo, and COA Commissioner Mario Lipana over their alleged involvement in anomalous and "ghost" flood control projects, on October 29, 2025. Jire Carreon/Rappler It’s been more than three months since the Marcos government vowed to go after officials allegedly involved in flood control corruption in July, but not a single person has been brought to detention, as of posting. There are lots of moving parts in this government-wide crackdown. At least four agencies and bodies – the Office of the Ombudsman, Department of Justice (DOJ), Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), and the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) – are holding separate probes into the alleged corruption. After each investigation, authorities are expected to file a complaint either with the Ombudsman or the DOJ. After assessment, the Ombudsman or justice officials may file criminal cases with the courts against those allegedly involved. It’s only after cases reach the courts that warrants may be issued. As a powerful constitutional body, the Ombudsman, apart from handling criminal offenses, may also fire or suspend government officials found administratively guilty. There’s only a slight complication on the ICI’s part, however, because the body only recommends complaints with the Ombudsman. Meaning, its submissions to the constitutional body are only considered “referrals,” not complaints. “To make the record straight, we cannot make any complaint, we cannot file a complaint under our mandate, we [can only refer]. So the complaint, the referrals, later on will be sworn to and subscribed to by DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon who will make it a complaint,” ICI Chairperson Andres Reyes Jr. explained. In this story, Rappler helps you track the development of each legal action filed against the actors involved in the multi-billion-peso corruption scandal. None yet Allegations: Violation of Republic Act (RA) No. 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, malversation through falsification of public documents, and violation of the Government Procurement Act Respondents: Former Bulacan 1st district engineer Henry Alcantara, former district engineer Brice Hernandez, former assistant district engineer Jaypee Mendoza, Sarah Discaya and Ma. Roma Angeline Rimando (St. Timothy Construction), Mark Arevalo (Wawao Builders), Sally Santos (SYMS Construction Trading), and Robert Imperio (IM Construction Corporation). Details: This complaint stems from five allegedly anomalous flood control projects in Malolos, Hagonoy, Bulakan, and Baliwag, Bulacan. Status : Pending with the Ombudsman Allegations: Alleged violation of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, indirect bribery, and malversation of public funds Respondents: The initial complaints include Senators Chiz Escudero, Jinggoy Estrada, and Joel Villanueva, as well as former representative Zaldy Co, among others. Details : DOJ Undersecretary Jesse Andres said on Tuesday, November 4, that they have five complaints undergoing preliminary investigation. Meaning, the prosecutors are now in the stage of issuing subpoenas to respondents in these complaints. If the respondents fail to submit their counter-affidavits, the prosecutors may immediately submit the cases for resolution. They can either indict (file charges) against the respondents or not. Status : Pending with the DOJ; for preliminary investigation Allegations: Malversation of public funds, falsification of documents Respondents: “Twelve people were charged, plus the Silverwolves Corporation for the La Union case. Nine [people] for the Davao Occidental case, plus St. Timothy [Corporation] and Sarah Discaya,” Dizon said. Details: The first complaint was filed over a P96.5-million flood control project in La Union, awarded to Silverwolves Construction Corporation. The second stems from two projects in Davao Occidental worth P89.73 million each, or a total of P179.5 million, both awarded to St. Timothy Corporation. Status: Pending with the Ombudsman Allegations : Criminal — graft, malversation, falsification, and alleged violation of  the Government Procurement Reform Act; Administrative — violation of Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees and Civil Service Rules and Regulations. Respondents : Resigned Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co, Gerald Pacanan, Gene Ryan Altea, Ruben Santos Jr., Dominic Serrano, Felisardo Casuno, Timojen Sacar, Montrexis Tamayo, Juliet Calvo, Dennis Abagon, Lerma Cayco, Grace Lopez, Friedrich Karl Camero, Aderma Angelie Alcazar, Cesar Buenaventura, Consuelo Aldo, Noel Cao, Anthony Ngo, and other potential respondents linked to construction contracts of Sunwest. Details : ICI flagged the alleged use of “grossly substandard” materials in the construction of a road dike along the Mag-Asawang Tubig River in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro. The P289.5-million flood control project in Oriental Mindoro was bagged by Sunwest Inc., a business conglomerate based in Albay co-founded by Co. Status : Pending with the Ombudsman for further evaluation Allegations: Plunder, graft, bribery, and corruption of public officers Respondents: Estrada, Villanueva, Co, Commission on Audit Commissioner Mario Lipana, former Caloocan 2nd District representative Mary Mitzi Cajayon-Uy, and former DPWH undersecretary Roberto Bernardo Details: The recommendations were based on the sworn affidavits and corroborating evidence of dismissed DPWH officials Alcantara, Hernandez, and Mendoza. Status: Pending with the Ombudsman for further evaluation Allegations: Criminal — graft, malversation, falsification, alleged violation of Presidential Decree No. 1759, and the Government Procurement Reform Act; Administrative — grave misconduct, gross dishonesty, conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service, or for any violation of Republic Act (RA) No. 6713 or Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees Respondents: Criminal — Alcantara, Hernandez, Ernesto Galang, Mendoza, John Michael Ramos, Irene Ontingco, Joshua Blitz Roxas, Topnotch president Eumir Villanueva; Administrative — former DPWH undersecretaries Bernardo and Maria Catalina Cabral, Alcantara, Hernandez, Galang, Mendoza, Ramos, Ontingco, Roxas, and Bernardo Villafuerte Details : The ICI report stems from a P72.3-million riverbank protection structure in Bagong Silang, Plaridel, Bulacan. According to the body, a Commission on Audit (COA) report revealed that no structure was constructed at the location specified in the approved bid plans. Status: Pending with the Ombudsman for further evaluation Allegations : Criminal — graft, malversation, falsification, alleged violation of Presidential Decree No. 1759, and the Government Procurement Reform Act; Administrative — grave misconduct, gross dishonesty, conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service, or for any violation of Republic Act (RA) No. 6713 or Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees Respondents : Criminal — Alcantara, Brice Hernandez, Jaime R. Hernandez, Ernesto Galang, John Carlo C. Rivera, John Michael E. Marcos, Claudine Magdalene Magsakay, Ericka Justine P. Chico, and Topnotch and Beam’s general manager Allan Payawal; Administrative — former DPWH undersecretaries Bernardo and Maria Catalina Cabral, Alcantara, Brice Hernandez, Jaime Hernandez, Galang, Rivera, Marcos, Magsakay, and Chico. Details : The issue is related to the P95-million flood control project in Barangay Bambang, Bocaue, Bulacan. The project is a joint venture between Topnotch Catalyst Builders Incorporated and Beam Team Developer Specialist Incorporated. Citing a report from COA, ICI said that no structure was constructed at the location specified in the approved bid plans. Status : Pending with the Ombudsman for further evaluation. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

title: What’s a flood control project, anyway?
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Floods are a part of the world’s natural water cycle and cannot be totally prevented, but the damage they inflict can be controlled effectively with the right methods, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) . Flood control projects are one of those methods. They are defined by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) as engineering works that, individually or in combination, provide flood protection and reduce flood damage. But does that mean flood control projects only remove or keep out rainwater? Not quite. In a technical sense, the projects that the DPWH categorizes as flood control structures in its 2022 guidelines only include those that hold, pump, and divert flood water, increase an area’s flood capacity, retain excess water, and enhance flood flow. This follows the more traditional definition of flood management, as described in a 2014 study of the National Academy of Science and Technology . But the same study argues that flood control must also consider other water-related disasters, like landslides, storm surges, dam breaks, and high tides. Because of this, structures that protect land areas  from collapsing and that keep out water from the sea can be considered flood control projects. In 2024, the DPWH also released guidelines for comprehensive water management in flood control projects, which means these projects now also “conserve and utilize water beneficially” through irrigation, water supply, and power generation. This wider definition of flood control is reflected in President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s flood control list, which includes drainage, sediment control, rainwater storage, and river, coastal, and slope protection projects. With this extensive list and the DPWH having individual flood control master plans for each of the country’s 18 major river basins, it can be hard to keep track of flood control projects from region to region. So, how do different types of flood control projects work, and what do they look like? Here’s a list that you can use to spot and scrutinize the ones you can probably find in your own community. PAGASA defines a flood as “an abnormal progressive rise in the water level of a stream that may result in the over­flowing by the water of the normal confines of the stream with the subsequent inundation of areas which are not normally submerged.” There are two main reasons for this, according to the government agency: the accumulation of rainwater and water overflowing from bodies of water, especially given the abundance of rivers in the country. The 2003 flood control planning manual made by the DPWH and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) says that flood control structures that prevent rivers from overflowing do so by improving how these rivers flow. This is done by removing sediment from their bottoms, making them wider, or straightening them. The national government is in charge of these kinds of works in major or principal river basins, according to guidelines of the DPWH. Projects around local rivers and creeks are expected to be funded and undertaken by the local governments where they are found. But when both river and rainwater end up accumulating in crucial areas like urban hubs and residences, certain flood control structures are used to drain this excess water. To do this, drainage systems use different components to remove rainwater by intercepting it and then transporting it somewhere safe. Open channels like canals and other openings like storm drains capture floodwater. Culverts and other pipes, with the help of pumps for easier transportation, can connect floodwaters in local areas to places where the excess water will not cause damage. So where does this excess water go? They can go to major waterways like rivers, or man-made structures can be built to store this water and either release it later or use it for other purposes. Excess water can be stored temporarily and then gradually released. For example, the five-story detention tank in Bonifacio Global City releases collected water into the Pasig River and Manila Bay. Floodwaters can also be stored permanently in water impounding systems so they can be used for irrigation, household water supplies, electricity generation, soil erosion prevention, and other water resource applications. They can be integrated with other flood control projects like dams, dikes, and diversion channels. But water is not the only substance that flows during floods. Sediment like soil can be dragged along with the current and end up clogging rivers and other waterways if left unattended. Because of this, structures that prevent sediment from accumulating are part of flood control. Sabo engineering is the term used to describe the erosion and sediment control measures used by the DPWH . Works like this include specialized dams that trap sediment and debris so that they do not clog waterways or damage infrastructure downstream, especially when flood currents are strong. Other maintenance works like desilting and declogging are also considered flood control projects by the DPWH . When floods hit, other water-related disasters like storm surges can occur, along with high tides. Preventing this seawater from spilling over into coastal communities is part of flood control. Also, flooding can weaken riverbeds, areas along the coast, and sloping landforms, according to the DPWH and JICA ’s 2003 flood control planning manual . To prevent landslides and the collapse of land forms near bodies of water, these protection projects are part of flood control. But infrastructure is not the only way to address the country’s flood problem. Aside from these structural measures, flood management also has non-structural measures, which use other types of technologies like mapping, forecasting, monitoring, evacuation, resettlement, and conservation practices to control floods. A 2022 study from the University of the Philippines, which looked into the country’s flood control projects from the Hispanic period to the present, found that the DPWH focused too much on “costly structural solutions or risk reduction strategies” that were rendered ineffective if not finished or maintained. “The most effective solutions in mitigating the effects of flooding are mostly non-structural in nature,” the study said. “[But since] there are situations where structural solutions are inevitable…a combination of strategies with focus more on risk avoidance strategies should be considered.” – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

title: [OPINION] Flood control beyond concrete: Auditing the builders and breakers
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Deputy House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos’s remark that third-party audits are indispensable for flood control projects — since legislators cannot credibly investigate themselves — is a timely and necessary call. This candor matters because acknowledging the gap in oversight is the first step toward fixing it. As co-Founder of the Masungi Georeserve Foundation , I have worked with rangers, communities, and partners to protect and restore the Upper Marikina Watershed, a critically threatened watershed that supports millions of Filipinos. What I’ve witnessed is how environmental destruction and flood control failures are two sides of the same coin, both enabled by the same systemic weaknesses in oversight and accountability. (READ: Protecting Masungi: What the rock means to geologists ) The Ombudsman’s recent dismissal of Bohol’s Sagbayan mayor and multiple Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) officials over Captain’s Peak Resort in the protected Chocolate Hills demonstrates what accountability with real consequences looks like. The Ombudsman found these officials guilty of grave misconduct and gross neglect of duty for allowing a resort to operate without required permits in a UNESCO World Heritage site and national treasure. (READ: How messy governance, paperwork allowed a resort in Chocolate Hills ) This case reached resolution because it went past internal agency processes and was proactively initiated by the Ombudsman itself. Had it remained within DENR’s systems, it would likely have joined the countless reversion cases still pending after years of bureaucratic delays. The same pattern repeats in threatened watersheds like Masungi, where resorts continue operating illegally despite repeated violations, because enforcement depends on the very agencies that initially failed to prevent the damage. This illustrates why Marcos’s call for third-party audits resonates: agencies cannot effectively police their own failures. But audits and reports cannot be ceremonial. They must come with penalties, sanctions, permit suspensions, or criminal charges. Without real consequences, bad actors simply wait out public attention or slip through bureaucratic loopholes. How we act now will determine what this country will tolerate, even after headlines fade. We need institutionalized checks and balances with teeth. Unfortunately, there are already attempts to shield critical environmental information from public scrutiny. The invocation of the Data Privacy Act to withhold Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) for projects with major ecological consequences is deeply concerning. EIAs are not personal records; they are public interest documents. Withholding them erodes accountability and undermines the ability of communities, scientists, and watchdogs to evaluate the true costs of proposed projects. Full public disclosure of environmental impact assessments, audit findings, contracts, and permit histories must be non-negotiable. Pasig City Mayor Vico Sotto has shown how transparency curtails corruption. His first reforms redirected funds to essential services by removing procurement opacity. Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong has repeatedly warned of the high percentage of pocketed money in government contracts; it should not take whistleblowers to make this visible. The question is: how can whistleblowers, reformist mayors, prototype solutions like Masungi and those tasked with oversight be protected and supported? In a climate where exposing corruption can end careers or worse, legal safeguards, dedicated funding, and institutional backing for watchdogs and innovators fighting against the tide are essential. We do not have the luxury of time to wait for generational departmental reform. The climate crisis is already here, delivering stronger typhoons, more erratic rainfall, and unprecedented flooding. Every year of delay means more lives lost, more livelihoods destroyed, and more public funds wasted on reactive measures. Given entrenched corruption, relying solely on departmental reform is unrealistic. Even well-intentioned agencies are often constrained by political interference, limited resources, or conflicting mandates. This is why a dedicated, nationally mandated commission is essential now — one with the legal authority, enforcement strength, financial capacity, and independence to oversee both flood-control efforts and watershed protection with urgency and integrity. We already have a precedent: the Climate Change Commission (CCC), created to coordinate climate policy at the highest levels. But the CCC’s experience shows that structure alone is not enough — adequate funding and genuine decision-making power are critical. Flood control is not just about concrete. Grey infrastructure such as dikes, drainage channels, pumping stations, and floodgates, works only if green infrastructure — healthy watersheds, intact forests, functioning wetlands — is equally protected. This is not an abstract environmental argument; it is a practical engineering and fiscal one. Flood-control systems are designed with assumptions about how much water the surrounding landscape will absorb, slow, and release. When watersheds are degraded — through quarrying, illegal logging, land speculation, or poorly executed reforestation — those assumptions collapse. Slopes destabilize, sediment clogs waterways, and flood peaks rise. Grey infrastructure is then forced to handle far more water and debris than it was designed for, driving up maintenance costs and shortening its lifespan. Neglect the green, and you sabotage the grey. Quarry operators, illegal loggers, land speculators, and other destructive actors in watershed areas must therefore face the same level of rigorous, enforceable audits as the largest flood control contractors. When we combine taxpayer-funded programs with international investments, the total funding for flood control and green infrastructure runs into hundreds of billions annually. Yet these flows often have fewer safeguards than emergency relief. Large-scale environmental and flood-control spending — where poor execution can undermine resilience for decades — suffers from fragmented oversight, inconsistent transparency, and little long-term outcome tracking. For investments of this scale, “trust us” is not a policy. They deserve rigorous safeguards precisely because they are intended to prevent the next crisis, not just respond to it. Grey and green infrastructure together form the backbone of our disaster defense. When one is compromised, the whole system falters. Only last week, I stood on top of a mountain in the outskirts of Metro Manila with a high-ranking official from an international agency. Looking out over the valleys and waterways below, he lamented: “The Philippines is not poor. It’s that billions are squandered. If corruption could be curtailed, you would find there is plenty for important services.” Curtailing corruption in these sectors is a matter of public safety and climate survival. Every inflated contract, every unmonitored project, and every ignored violation weakens the nation’s defenses against the very disasters these funds are meant to prevent. The choice before us is clear: embed rigorous safeguards now, or accept that we will keep pouring resources into systems that enrich the few while leaving millions at risk. – Rappler.com Ann Dumaliang co-founded the Masungi Georeserve Foundation, continuing a 30-year fight to restore and protect a limestone karst landscape, and now leading efforts to rehabilitate portions of the Upper Marikina Watershed against inertia and illegal encroachment. Fajardo(Member)—took their oath of office before Court of Appeals Justice Pedro Corales, on September 15, 2026. Presidential Communications Offi MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit Fraud Audit Office (COA FAO) on Friday, October 11, submitted its fifth batch of reports on the flood control anomaly in Bulacan to the Independent Commission for Infrastructure. The reports covered four construction of barriers to serve as flood protection of three towns in Bulacan. All of the four projects – funded by the Department of Public Works and Highways’ Bulacan First District Engineering Office – were tagged by COA as ghost projects. The first report included a P96.5 million “riverbank protection structure” in Barangay San Roque, Baliuag, Bulacan contracted by M3 Konstract Corporation. “COA proceeded to inspect the site identified by DPWH, where it found an existing structure that already had several defects and cracks. Worse, the existing structure is for a different project altogether. COA also inspected the original approved location and found a structure attributable to a different project as well,” the audit team said. For this project, among those found liable are: For the second and third projects, SYMS Construction and Trading was supposed to build a P92.67-million flood structure in Barangay Manatal in Pandi, and a P74.112-million riverbank protection structure along Balagtas River in Barangay San Juan in Balagtas. But according to COA, the payments to the contractor were given Notices of Disallowance due to numerous violations. “DPWH-Bulacan First DEO representatives pinpointed a different project site to COA. Again, no explanation was provided why the location was changed. At the pinpointed location, COA saw an unfinished structure with exposed steel bars, formworks, and sheet piles. COA also noted the absence of any workers or equipment at the location during the inspection,” the report said in relation to the Pandi project. Those found liable are Alcantara, Hernandez, Galang, Ramos, Project Engineer Lemuel Ephraim Roque, Engineer Jolo Mari Tayao, and Sally Santos of SYMS Construction Trading. In the Balagtas project, COA said that the project’s original location did not have a flood structure. In the site pointed by the DPWH, the auditors found an existing structure that failed to meet project specifications due to unsuitable materials used. “COA discovered that based on DPWH’s own database, the project was tagged as on-going, yet full payment was already made to the contractor,” the auditors said. Those named liable are Alcantara, Hernandez, Galang, Ramos, Ontingco, Buendia, Engineer Michelle Cruz, and SYMS’ Santos. Meanwhile, the fourth project was contracted by Amethyst Horizon Builders and Gen. Contractor and Development Corporation for P96.5 million. This involves the construction of a riverbank protection structure along Balagtas River supposedly located in Barangay Dalig in Balagtas. However, the identified location on the documents was different from the site where the DPWH-Bulacan First DEO led the auditing team. “During COA’s inspection a flood control project was seen at the approved location but DPWH-Bulacan First DEO a project at another location. At the pinpointed location, COA found a flood control structure which did not match the approved plan. Again, DPWH offered no justification why the location was changed,” the audit team said. Held liable for the anomalous project are Alcantara, Hernandez, Galang, Ontingco, Ramos, Mendoza, Cruz, Engineer Jasmine Jean Gonzaga, and Rochelle Campos of Amethyst Horizon Builders and Gen. Contractor and Development Corp. Based on its count, the COA FAO said it had already turned over nine fraud audit reports to the Office of the Ombudsman and 12 to the ICI. The COA initiated the fraud audit on flood control projects after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered a performance review of the projects amid corruption allegations. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

MANILA, Philippines – Different government agencies have uncovered at leaast 421 ghost flood control projects across the country, Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vince Dizon said in a press conference on Thursday, October 9. Dizon said the projects were discovered after the validation of around 8,000 DPWH projects. The validation was conducted in coordination with the Department of National Defense, Armed Forces of the Philippines, Philippine National Police, and the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development. Dizon did not disclose the total value or funding period of the ghost projects but said most were located in Luzon. Congressional probes, as well as surprise ocular inspections of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in August, have pointed to non-existent flood control projects in Bulacan . The Commission on Audit has submitted fraud audit reports to the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) where it flagged alleged anomalous flood control projects also in Bulacan. Meanwhile, the ICI recommended that the DPWH reduce the spending authority of its regional and district offices for civil works projects. Under current rules, DPWH regional engineering offices can approve projects worth up to P400 million. The ICI wants to slash the cap to P200 million. For district engineering offices, the spending limit is P150 million, which the ICI proposes to reduce to P75 million. The recommendation, addressed to the DPWH and dated October 4, was made public on Thursday, October 9. In 2022, under then-DPWH secretary Manuel Bonoan, the department increased the level of authority for the procurement of civil works for its regional and district offices. Prior to Bonoan’s directive, district offices could only approve projects up to P100 million, while regional offices were limited to P300 million. The table below shows the changes in spending authority levels and the ICI’s proposed adjustments: The recommendation comes amid mounting concerns over corruption within DPWH district and regional offices. The Bulacan 1st District Engineering Office, in particular, has been under scrutiny following reports of collusion among district engineers, politicians, and contractors. Dismissed Bulacan assistant district engineer Brice Hernandez even revealed that the projects under the 1st DEO from 2019 to 2025 were all substandard. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

title: Carlos Loria, Co rival, bagged P2.3-B flood control deals before 2025 win
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Photo by Sam Calleja/Rappler ALBAY, Philippines – Albay 2nd District Representative Carlos “Caloy” Loria was considered a political neophyte when he won the May 2025 election against Zaldy Co ’s brother and former Ako Bicol (AKB) Partylist representative Christopher Co . However, well before his congressional run, Makapa Corporation — a company Loria founded — had been securing billions in government contracts in the Bicol region. Between 2021 and 2023, Loria’s company secured a series of lucrative contracts with the Department of Public Works and Highways, marking a period of substantial business growth. The firm won over 20 flood control projects in Albay and the 2nd district of Sorsogon, amounting to some P2.39 billion. Being a DPWH contractor is not inherently wrong before entering politics. Yet for someone who campaigned on “real change” and a break from entrenched political habits, the extent of his firm’s DPWH ties raises questions about how different he truly is from those he sought to replace. ( READ: Firms tied to Zaldy Co bag P2.38B to fix floods they worsened in Albay ) Bicolana Gabriela regional coordinator Nica Ombao said the promises of “real change for all Filipinos” require scrutinizing a politician’s background, “especially where their money or wealth comes from — these assets and liabilities, where they originated.” Ombao stressed her difficulty of believing Loria’s anti-corruption stance. “It is hard to say that you are against corruption when you are speaking up against DPWH issues, but you have actually already been a part of the DPWH’s anomalies. It is very difficult to accept and value this promised ‘real change’ if they themselves have already benefited from the old, destructive, and exploitative system that we have now,” she said. The large cumulative value of the contracts secured by his company appears to contradict Loria’s recent Facebook post , in which he said the “best flood control” requires no billions, only to “respect and protect mother nature.” The “ Rosaloria” tandem – composed of Loria and Albay Governor Noel Rosal – ran in the 2025 election under the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino (PDP–Laban), the political party of detained former president Rodrigo Duterte whose administration implemented some of the controversial flood control projects in the country. One of the flood control projects under Makapa in Albay was the rehabilitation of the structure along the Quinale River. This river marks the boundary between Polangui and Libon, two of the towns hardest hit during the flooding caused by Severe Tropical Storm Kristine (Trami) in 2024. ( READ: Thirsty Kristine victims in Albay village forced to boil, drink floodwater for survival ) Rappler’s review of DPWH and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) data showed that Makapa secured a contract worth P125,336,435.30 for the flood control project that was declared finished in 2023. Despite this significant public spending, residents report that the flooding problem in the area remains unsolved. They continue to suffer the burden of ineffective flood control projects that are often repaired and rehabilitated due to their poor quality. “They measured it and added more, but nothing is happening,” said Morly Ortiz, a Polangui resident who has lived near the Quinale River for over 15 years and experienced multiple floods. “We just want effective flood control so we can finally be safe from the water.” Like Ortiz, Myrna Mirandilla of Libon, lamented the loss of their harvest, especially during the onslaught of Kristine. “The water kept rising, up to our necks, so during the last storm, I had to leave with my grandchildren because we were afraid we’d drown,” said Mirandilla in Filipino. “When I returned home, there were no more walls, no roof, all our belongings were gone, and even our farm animals were washed away.” Mirandilla, who lives with her farmer husband and family, explained that they cannot move to a safer location because their house is close to the fields where her husband works. The Kilusan ng Magbubukid sa Pilipinas (KMP) in Bicol has blamed anomalous flood control projects for the wide-ranging damage experienced by residents and farmers like Mirandilla’s family. “The experience of Bicol last year, when it was battered by storms like Enteng, Kristine, and Pepito, brought widespread, deep, and prolonged flooding — this is a naked truth,” said KMP-Bicol in Filipino in a statement . “The storm is not the cause of the intensified effect, but the vulnerability of the people, which is worsened by the failure of flood control projects, corruption, unfinished works, and sub-standard construction.” In 2024, the Department of Agriculture reported over P2.1 billion in agricultural losses due to Kristine nationwide, with Albay alone accounting for P403.8 million. Libon, considered the rice granary of Albay, suffered heavy damage. A study by the Harvard Humanitarian Initiative (HHI) showed that while Kristine victims are accustomed to calamities, they are still far from being better prepared. Dr. Vincenzo Bollettino, director of HHI’s Resilient Communities program, said, “Despite facing frequent and intense typhoons, Bicol’s lower preparedness highlights a critical disconnect between experience and readiness.” This lack of preparedness and the inefficient flood control leave vulnerable families gravely exposed to disasters and reliant on officials for post-storm help. This reliance, however, often intersects with politics. In Loria’s case, his relief program, CALinga ni Loria , often provided aid to communities battered by the floods that resulted, in part, from the flood control projects in which his firm, Makapa, was involved. This program became his main visibility effort, accelerating his campaign since 2024, with relief operation posts on social media using hashtags like #CAL25 that signaled his bid for public office. For Mirandilla, however, the best help Albayanos can get is not a post-disaster appearance, but proper, effective projects that safeguard their lives. “If the flood control was properly done, we wouldn’t be flooded, and we wouldn’t have to suffer,” she emphasized. Makapa’s operations are not limited to construction; like the Co family’s businesses in Albay, Makapa also runs quarrying operations, an industry widely blamed by Albayanos for worsened flooding . The company operates quarries near the boundary of Ligao City and Guinobatan town, an area already known for its susceptibility to flooding. ( READ: In typhoon-hit Bicol, political clans aiding victims backed projects blamed for flooding ) A satellite image from Google Maps clearly shows the signage for Makapa’s quarry operations in Baligang, Ligao City. Furthermore, satellite images spanning several years from Google Earth Pro illustrate the environmental damage caused by these operations in the area. Asked about his company’s future involvement in public contracts, Loria said in a 2024 public forum that he would divest from Makapa and that the company would cease participating in contract biddings for projects in Albay. “I will divest from Makapa — that’s the first thing that I will do. I will divest and I will not be there personally. Makapa Corporation will not engage in projects in Albay. It would be better that it operates in Manila, where projects are worth billions,” Loria said in Bicolano. Based on the SEC documents, Loria and his spouse, Roslyn Loria, were still registered as Makapa’s majority shareholders during their latest annual meeting in March. Loria held 59% of the total shares, amounting to P126.850 million, and his spouse held 20% of the total shares, amounting to P43 million. After several amendments to their records, the latest report in October already indicates that Loria and his wife were not included among Makapa’s shareholders. However, their two daughters, Patricia Karla Loria and Karla Nicole Loria Elvira, remain among the top shareholders, each holding 24% of the shares, amounting to P35.5 million each. Following Loria’s divestment, the total shares of Makapa Corporation decreased from P215 million in March to P148.15 million in October — a reduction of almost half. All other remaining registered shareholders are also related to Loria and his spouse. From 2021 to 2023, Makapa secured government contracts worth some P642.5 million in Albay’s 1st District, P665.3 million in the 2nd District, P445 million in the 3rd District, and P638.5 million in Sorsogon’s 2nd District. Despite several follow-ups, Rappler has yet to receive a response regarding the matter. We will update this story once Loria’s office provides a statement. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

title: How much is the government spending on flood control projects?
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. FLOOD. Commuters were forced to walk through flooded streets after continuous rain in Manila on July 24, 2024. Rappler Every typhoon season, thousands of Filipinos are affected by flooding. Floodwaters damage homes and properties, destroy crops , and disrupt businesses and livelihoods, especially in the agriculture sector. They paralyze transportation and force class suspensions . Flooding also continues to claim thousands of lives year after year. To address this problem, the government spends billions of pesos in taxpayers ’ money each year on flood management programs. But despite the ballooning budget, the problem of flooding remains unsolved. Here’s a look at how much the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has spent on flood control over the years: Over a span of 15 years, from 2011 to 2025, the government allocated P1.47 trillion for flood control and mitigation programs. In 2025, the DPWH received the second largest budget allocation at P1.007 trillion, just behind the education sector — which includes the Department of Education , state universities and colleges, the Commission on Higher Education , and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority — with P1.055 trillion. Based on the National Expenditure Program, the DPWH’s proposed budget was P900 billion. In the bicameral committee report, it ballooned to P1.034 billion. Ibon Foundation executive director Sonny Africa flagged the insertions made by lawmakers in the DPWH budget during the bicameral conference process, saying they were “widely suspected to be more pork barrel projects .” In a 2021 report, the Department of Justice said the DPWH and local government units received the highest number of corruption complaints among government agencies. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

title: [Vantage Point] Purging the flood control rot: Will Marcos Jr. sink or swim?
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Raphael Reyes/Rappler President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos in a defiant tone warned that “ no one, not even family members or political allies, will be spared ” from the investigation into corruption  allegations in the scandalous flood control projects. On September 11, 2025, he established the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) through Executive Order 94 . This three-member body will probe irregularities in flood control projects and all national government infrastructure works through the years. The President says being subjected to investigation is a way to determine innocence or guilt. His cousin House Speaker Martin Romualdez, who recently resigned his post, and close ally Representative Zaldy Co of the Ako Bicol partylist are among those implicated in the anomalous flood control projects. The move could be of historical importance. No other sitting Philippine president before Marcos Jr. had called for a probe on massive corruption, vowed to end it, and hold perpetrators accountable. Through the years, the focus of corruption probes has always been the executive, with Congress as the accusing party. But will the President’s bravado match the results? Fairness cannot be expected of either legislative chamber because, as the President pointed out, “Maraming nababanggit na senador … marami ring nababanggit na congressman (Many senators have been named…and many congressmen have also been mentioned).” “ Kaya sinasabi ng mga tao, bakit naman nag-iimbestiga sila (That is why the people are saying, why are they doing the investigation), but they are investigating themselves, which is always a little bit of a difficult situation na (already, and) it’s hard to be fair,” Marcos Jr. said in citing the reason for the formation of an independent probe. The ICI is composed of retired Supreme Court justice Andres Reyes Jr. , who is tasked to carry out the investigation within the bounds of law and the Constitution; former DPWH secretary Rogelio Singson, who is expected to provide the engineering and technical expertise required in assessing the questionable projects; Rossana Fajardo, a certified public accountant who has the inquisitive and critical mind of a forensic accountant that could dissect the financial aspects of the anomalous projects, and Mayor Benjamin Magalong, a former police officer who will put together the evidence needed to secure conviction of those involved. Vantage Point sees the creation of the ICI as more than a political maneuver — it is a crucial corrective measure to address a flawed system where congressional investigations have historically produced more spectacle than substance. The creation of such a body recognizes a central truth: accountability cannot thrive in institutions where self-interest and political posturing overwhelm the pursuit of justice. Congress, for all its constitutional oversight powers, has repeatedly fallen into the trap of using inquiries as platforms for partisan warfare rather than venues for truth-finding. The ongoing hearings on flood control projects illustrate this dysfunction vividly. Instead of a sober dissection of systemic flaws — why billions are poured into projects that either collapse prematurely or fail to mitigate flooding — what the public sees are legislators jousting for soundbites, trading accusations, and conveniently steering scrutiny away from allies. This erodes trust and, more critically, distracts from the evidence trail that could lead to prosecution. By contrast, an independent commission carries both the neutrality and institutional focus that Congress lacks. The commission can cut through political noise and track where the money went, who profited, and why institutional safeguards failed. Its singular mandate will be to map the anatomy of corruption in flood control — without the burden of protecting political patrons or the need to spin narratives for reelection. Critics will argue that Congress has the constitutional duty of oversight, and that relinquishing investigations to a commission undermines this check-and-balance system. This argument, while sound on paper, ignores political reality. The same lawmakers who authorized, lobbied for, or benefitted from flood control projects cannot credibly be the ones to investigate their own complicity. Oversight becomes farcical when the overseer has a vested interest in muddying the trail. What the nation needs is not a duplicative circus of simultaneous inquiries but a disciplined, impartial probe that will command the confidence of the public and withstand judicial scrutiny. For this reason, Congress should step aside — not in abdication of its duty, but in recognition of its conflict of interest. It can play a constructive role later, by legislating reforms based on the ICI’s findings: tightening procurement rules, creating stricter monitoring systems, and enacting safeguards against collusion between contractors and officials. Flood control projects have long been the pork barrel of public works, bleeding billions from the treasury with little to show in terms of real flood mitigation. Marcos’ move to establish an independent commission is thus an opportunity to break this cycle. Congress must resist the temptation to grandstand and instead allow the process to run its course. The Filipino public is tired of inquiries that end in stalemate and scandal fatigue. I’m giving the ICI the benefit of the doubt. It offers a chance — perhaps the last in this cycle of corruption — to pierce the veil of impunity. Congress should allow it to do its work unimpeded. Its role will come later, not as prosecutor, but as reformer: to legislate stricter procurement safeguards, stronger monitoring systems, and airtight penalties for collusion. History offers sobering lessons. The Fertilizer Fund scam hearings conducted by the Senate Committee on Agriculture. Congress hearings in 2006 exposed how billions meant for farmers were siphoned off, yet not a single mastermind was meaningfully punished. The 2007 inquiry into the Philippine National Broadband Network controversy (also referred to as the NBN–ZTE deal or NBN–ZTE mess) became a theater of walkouts and exposés, but no one went to jail despite overwhelming evidence of bribery. The Priority Development Assistance Fund scandal, also called the PDAF scam or the pork barrel scam — perhaps the most infamous — was exposed in 2013 and showcased lawmakers grilling Janet Napoles on prime-time television, even as many of those who had benefitted from her schemes managed to slip away untouched. In all these cases, congressional probes yielded publicity, not justice. If Congress refuses to yield, then history will judge it once more as a body obsessed with theatrics and prone to misrepresentation. If Marcos weakens the ICI, he will be condemned as just another president unwilling to confront entrenched and systemic corruption. But if both Congress and the Palace do what is right, the nation may finally see a corruption probe that delivers results instead of ratings. The independent commission to probe anomalies in flood control projects is both bold and necessary. For decades, congressional investigations have carried the illusion of accountability, but their record betrays a troubling pattern: more smoke than fire, more grandstanding than justice. The ongoing flood control investigation shows the same symptoms. Lawmakers thunder about corruption, but their questions often pivot to protecting allies or undermining rivals. The spectacle dominates headlines while the technical heart of the matter — where the money went, how contracts were rigged, which officials facilitated the graft — remains obscured. Worse, the very lawmakers implicated in the misuse of flood control funds now position themselves as truth-seekers, further eroding the credibility of the entire exercise. But a word of warning must also be addressed to the President: creating a commission is only half the battle. Filipinos have seen too many “independent” bodies neutered into irrelevance. The Agrava Commission on Ninoy Aquino’s assassination , the Melo Commission on political killings, and the Sabio Panel on military corruption all began with high expectations but ended with watered-down reports and no real accountability. Each became a symbol of how commissions can be used to defuse public anger while protecting the powerful. Marcos cannot afford that outcome. He must give the flood control commission teeth — subpoena powers, prosecutorial backing, and full public transparency. Anything less, and it will be dismissed as just another political gimmick. More than that, this commission will test Marcos Jr.’s political capital and his break from the Duterte patronage networks that once nurtured players like the Discayas. If the commission fearlessly investigates not just contractors but the politicians who enabled them — whether allies in Congress or remnants of the Duterte’s camp — it will signal a real shift in how corruption is confronted. If it tiptoes around the powerful, it will expose the President’s reformist stance as hollow. In the end, Marcos faces a defining choice. He can allow the commission to become the hammer that finally smashes the flood control syndicates, or he can let it wither into yet another dusty report in the Palace archives. His legacy hinges on this: will he be remembered as the president who cleaned up flood control, or as another chief executive who promised reform but shielded the guilty and protected the very syndicates he vowed to dismantle? The stakes could not be higher. This is not just about flood control; it is about whether the President can finally redraw the battle lines of accountability in Philippine governance. Marcos Jr. faces a test of leadership that will force him to conquer the rising floodwaters. Will he purge the rot in flood control or drown in the same tide of impunity that engulfed every president before him? His legacy hangs in the balance. – Rappler.com  How does this make you feel?

title: Zero budget for flood control projects. Does it mean zero corruption too?
text: MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has scrapped the P252-billion funding for locally funded flood control projects in its revised 2026 budget proposal . The DPWH also trimmed P3 billion worth of duplicate or completed projects, including overlapping road sections, rock netting, and cat’s eye and stud installations. This brings the agency’s proposed budget down to P625.8 billion from the initial P881 billion. But does this mean corruption is out of the picture? Rappler multimedia reporter Patrick Cruz reports. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

Unlike road projects or buildings, flood-control works often lie beneath the surface. Once completed, they’re buried under soil or hidden beneath water — making inspection difficult, if not impossible, for ordinary citizens. In essence, it is a digital ledger distributed across multiple computers or “nodes.” Every transaction recorded in it is time-stamped, encrypted, and immutable — meaning once entered, it cannot be changed or deleted without the consensus of all participants. Open-Source Protocols The software code must be publicly available for inspection by independent information technology (IT) experts. Public Access Dashboard To ensure public scrutiny, citizens, journalists, and watchdogs can view non-sensitive data, such as project status, cost, and contractor. Automatic Flagging for COA and Ombudsman Because all government audit systems are interoperable via APIs (application programming interfaces), the flagged record automatically alerts the COA fraud detection unit, and the Ombudsman’s fact-finding office. Investigators can instantly trace who uploaded the original entry (timestamp + wallet ID + digital signature). No deletion, no excuses — accountability is cryptographically sealed. 6. Community Transparency and Citizen Oversight Citizens can open the public dashboard (e.g., dpwhfloodchain.gov.ph) and see: This not only deters collusion but builds public trust. If multiple Bulacan projects are flagged under the same regional engineer, analysts and journalists can map patterns of corruption across contracts. Blockchain cannot erase bad data — but it can trap it in the open. Through: A single falsified upload becomes an unerasable piece of evidence — one that exposes who, when, and how the lie was committed. This is the heart of blockchain’s anti-corruption utility — it turns cover-ups into breadcrumbs. The implications extend far beyond drainage canals and dikes. A blockchain-based ledger could be scaled across all infrastructure programs: Each project becomes part of a national integrity grid — a digital paper trail that cannot be burned. Even the most sophisticated networks of collusion crumble when data cannot be falsified. Globally, blockchain has already begun reshaping public accountability. In Estonia, land registries and public records are blockchain-secured, eliminating property fraud. Georgia uses blockchain to secure land titles , making document forgery impossible. In Colombia, pilot projects apply blockchain to public contracts, preventing alterations after bidding. Chile’s National Energy Commission adopted blockchain to verify energy pricing data, building trust among consumers. The Philippines can follow suit — but with a deeper purpose: not just efficiency, but redemption of a system long marred by patronage. Predictably, resistance will come from those who profit from opacity. Some lawmakers and local executives may argue that blockchain is “too technical,” “too costly,” or “too foreign.” In truth, the cost of inaction dwarfs any software expense. If even 5% of annual DPWH infrastructure outlays (roughly ₱80 billion) vanish into the corruption blackhole, then blockchain’s potential savings easily justify its investment. Another challenge is institutional inertia. Bureaucrats unaccustomed to transparency may fear automation. To counter this, training and pilot programs must be done in gradual phases, starting with high-risk sectors like flood control, where the payoff in credibility is immediate. The legal framework also matters. Legislation must classify blockchain records as official audit evidence, admissible in court and binding upon agencies. Under the current setup, witnesses risk retaliation, and affidavits often vanish or get rewritten. Blockchain flips this logic: every statement, evidence photo, or timestamped log uploaded becomes indelible. Even if a corrupt official later tries to coerce retraction, the digital record remains. This doesn’t just empower whistleblowers — it redefines testimonial truth. In effect, blockchain becomes the ultimate state witness: incorruptible, tireless, and immune to pressure. COA’s annual reports, though valuable, are often autopsies. They diagnose fraud after the patient — the public fund — has already died. In a blockchain system, COA becomes proactive, not reactive. Every disbursement is visible in real time. Anomalies trigger alerts the moment data diverges from verified ground truth. This transforms auditing from an afterthought to a continuous, living process. The collapse of public trust in government projects is as dangerous as physical flooding. Each scandal erodes faith in taxation, governance, and reform. Citizens begin to assume every canal is a cash conduit and every bridge, a payoff. By embedding transparency into code, blockchain begins to rebuild that faith. When ordinary Filipinos can open a web portal and see — verifiably — that ₱30 million was spent on work that has been truly and sufficiently completed, cynicism yields to accountability. Trust ceases to be rhetorical. It becomes mathematical. A national rollout must begin with pilot programs. Flood control in Central Luzon — the epicenter of recurring graft — is the ideal testbed. See related articles below: Parallel pilots can follow in the Visayas for coastal rehabilitation and in Mindanao for irrigation projects. Lessons learned can refine the architecture before nationwide expansion. Public-private collaboration is essential. Local tech startups, civil society groups, and academe must co-own the design — ensuring it serves citizens, not politicians and their cohorts. Ultimately, blockchain governance is not about technology, but moral architecture: coding honesty into the infrastructure of decision-making. This is the dream: Filipinos will finally have a country where every peso leaves a visible trail to something real and beneficial for everyone; where no lawmaker can “insert” projects without public knowledge; where COA’s database is not retrospective but real-time; where journalists can verify project truth in seconds, not years. In such a system, corruption cannot adapt because the system itself is immune to forgetting. Floodwaters may still rise from heavy rainfall, but this time, greed would not be the root cause. – Rappler.com I would like to thank my daughter Michelle for patiently teaching me about how blockchain works. Some lawmakers and local executives may argue that blockchain is “too technical,” “too costly,” or “too foreign.” In truth, the cost of inaction dwarfs any software expense. Blockchain flips this logic: every statement, evidence photo, or timestamped log uploaded becomes indelible. Even if a corrupt official later tries to coerce retraction, the digital record remains. Each scandal erodes faith in taxation, governance, and reform. Citizens begin to assume every canal is a cash conduit and every bridge, a payoff. By embedding transparency into code, blockchain begins to rebuild that faith. When ordinary Filipinos can open a web portal and see — verifiably — that ₱30 million was spent on work that has been truly and sufficiently completed, cynicism yields to accountability. Trust ceases to be rhetorical. It becomes mathematical. A national rollout must begin with pilot programs. Flood control in Central Luzon — the epicenter of recurring graft — is the ideal testbed. Lessons learned can refine the architecture before nationwide expansion. Public-private collaboration is essential. Local tech startups, civil society groups, and academe must co-own the design — ensuring it serves citizens, not politicians and their cohorts. Ultimately, blockchain governance is not about technology, but moral architecture: coding honesty into the infrastructure of decision-making. This is the dream: Filipinos will finally have a country where every peso leaves a visible trail to something real and beneficial for everyone; where no lawmaker can “insert” projects without public knowledge; where COA’s database is not retrospective but real-time; where journalists can verify project truth in seconds, not years. Floodwaters may still rise from heavy rainfall, but this time, greed would not be the root cause. – Rappler.com I would like to thank my daughter Michelle for patiently teaching me about how blockchain works. Members of Tindig Pilipinas, Nagkaisa Labor Coalition, Kalipunan ng Kilusang Masa, SIKLAB (Simbahan at Komunidad Laban sa Katiwalian), and Akbayan at the EDSA Shrine prepare to march to the People Power Monument in Quezon City to protest the widespread government corruption on September 11, 2025. Jire Carreon/Rappler MANILA, Philippines – Some wore white to indicate non-partisanship; some, black, to symbolize how government is as rotten as a grave. A woman in Tuguegarao, north of Manila, brought her entire family to the city park, to hopefully teach children not to stand idly by when wrong is being done. A man in Manila carried his dog, switching its name tag with a homemade placard that said, “ Nangangagat ng mga kora p (He bites corrupt people).” Runners and bikers were among the earliest to head to Luneta, the monument to the Philippine national hero, while celebrities showed up, shedding glamour for indignation. Others came on free rides provided by transport groups, while a motorcycle-hailing company offered discounts to passengers going to and coming from the rallies in Luneta and EDSA. At least one man literally wheeled himself — he was a person with disability confined to a wheelchair — across seven kilometers, from Cainta to where protesters were gathered along EDSA. Led mostly by young people, thousands of Filipinos marched in key cities across the Philippines on Sunday, September 21, to protest corruption in government, particularly in flood control projects. Quite poetically, those from up north in Luzon down to some parts of the Visayas marched against flood control project anomalies as rain poured, brought about by Super Typhoon Nando and the southwest monsoon. Student groups, sectoral organizations, religious groups, people of various political persuasions, and unaffiliated concerned citizens condemned those involved in the flood control scandal, while also acknowledging that the syndicate-like dealings had been made possible by a broken system that also needed fixing. More than condemning corruption that had reached dizzying amounts, and beyond calling for sustained vigilance among citizens, protesters cried for justice. Their demand was specific: jail the implicated lawmakers and other elected officials, Department of Public Works and Highways employees, and private contractors — or test the limits of an already outraged public. On social media, weeks before the rallies, a prevailing sentiment was to not just jail the corrupt, but to make them return what they stole from public coffers. There were even scares about protesters staging lightning rallies in posh subdivisions where so-called “policontractors” reside. “I think we did well. We surpassed our expectations,” said Kiko Aquino Dee, a spokesperson for the protest organizers at the People Power Monument, referring to the crowd estimate. Nationwide, an estimated 61,605 people joined protests against government corruption, the Philippine National Police reported. “Everybody was able to express their sentiments, their anger at the grave corruption happening in the Philippines, and we did it in a way that is peaceful. We did it in a way that rejected all of the things outside of the Constitution. We made our voices heard, we renewed our commitment to the spirit of People Power,” Dee told Rappler. The challenge after the rally is sustaining it, he said. “Definitely, the anger is still there. It’s up to us, organizers, to continue to give it venues to express it productively,” he added. While the rallies were organized primarily to protest the trillion-peso anomalies in flood control projects, various groups also took the opportunity to denounce endemic corruption in general, pointing out that both the families of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Vice President Sara Duterte were complicit. On Sunday, protesters also commemorated the 53rd anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law by President Ferdinand E. Marcos Sr., father of the incumbent. (READ: Marcos, the dictator’s son, backs September 21 protests vs flood control corruption ) Opposition politicians and celebrities joined the rallies and marches in Luneta in Manila and the People Power Monument in Quezon City, while rallies were also held in Baguio, Tuguegarao, Legazpi, Cebu, Dumaguete, Tacloban, Bacolod, Cagayan de Oro, Butuan, Cotabato, Marawi, and other key cities across the country. Some supporters of Vice President Duterte gathered near the main crowd of protesters on EDSA to call for Marcos’ ouster — which would mean Duterte would take over. (READ: Duterte: I am also corrupt ) The Vice President herself has refused to make public her assets list and to explain the alleged misuse of confidential funds allotted to her office. Her brother Paolo’s district in Davao City got P51 billion in flood control funds in the last half of their father’s presidency. During his State of the Nation Address in July, President Marcos warned against widespread corruption in flood control projects while Filipinos lose lives, livelihood, and belongings to constant floods. He told those involved, “ Mahiya naman kayo! (Be ashamed of yourselves!)” In early August, the President launched a website where citizens could check flood control projects and submit information on anomalous projects in their localities. A week before that, Rappler had already launched the FloodControlPH channel on the Rappler app to crowdsource leads for possible investigative pieces. Marcos identified 15 contractors which had cornered 1 in every 5 flood control projects across the country in the last 3 years, or under his administration. Five of them turned out to have bagged multi-billion-peso contracts despite not having enough capital . Later, he created the Independent Commission for Infrastructure that would investigate all possible public works and infrastructure corruption in the last 10 years. This means the probe covers the six years Rodrigo Duterte was president, when lawmakers, DPWH engineers, and private contractors were supposed to have perfected flood control fund misuse, which is deemed less detectable than those involving other infrastructure allocations. The Senate and the House of Representatives are conducting their own probes into the anomalous projects, although citizens have expressed doubts about where these would lead, as lawmakers are among those alleged to have benefited from corruption. A few DPWH engineers have either been dismissed from service or placed on preventive suspension , while several more are on the immigration lookout list . The Anti-Money Laundering Council has frozen hundreds of bank accounts linked to the persons being investigated. While some quarters are hoping that Sunday’s protest would snowball into something akin to the People Power Revolution of 1986 , others were concerned until when the rage would hold. What is clear to Obet Sumayao, the wheelchair-bound protester from Cainta, Rizal, is this: At least before he dies, he wants to see the crooks behind bars. – with reports from Aries Rufo Journalism Fellows 2025 , Roland Andam Jr., Iya Gozum, Gemma Mendoza, Paterno Esmaquel II/Rappler.com How does this make you feel?
