title: [OPINION] Flood control latest sign of government ‘greenwashing’
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Today marks the 16th anniversary of Tropical Storm Ondoy , which, in many ways, first opened the eyes of the Filipino nation to the reality of the climate crisis. Still, it took until earlier this year for the reported climate budget to exceed P1 trillion, or more than double of the previous year’s allocation. This seemed like a good sign that the entire government was finally ramping up its climate actions. However, from what we know now, it turns out it was too good to be true. Congressional sessions and agency meetings over the years have mostly emphasized the leading roles of agencies such as the Climate Change Commission (CCC) and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources in climate action. The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is not mentioned nearly as often, yet it is the agency with by far the largest share of the domestic climate budget. It has 89% of the allotment under the 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA) . Over P350 billion from its P1-trillion allocation was given to flood control projects, a slight increase from 2024. Today, the DPWH finds itself at the epicenter of the worst corruption scandal in recent years because of the anomalies related to flood control. Many across the nation took to the streets last Sunday, September 21, demanding an end to the culture of impunity that has manifested many times before. In reference to a previous Rappler op-ed , these peaceful protests may be the “tipping point” for a renewed nationwide demand for genuine good governance. Because there may be more in this climate budget that needs to be looked into. In the 2025 GAA, the DPWH budget also featured more than P330 billion for the construction of new roads, ports, and other infrastructure to “climate-resilient design standards.” An additional P216.8 billion was allotted for retrofitting assets and capital “to protect against climate change and climate variability”; examining the document showed these assets and capital largely also pertain to roads. The reputation of road construction and repairs in the Philippines is perhaps even more notorious than flood control projects. Given the similarities in issues often observed among these projects, conducting an extensive national investigation on road repair and construction projects should also be done under the current administration. This context has influenced the Department of Agriculture to begin an audit of all farm-to-market roads since 2021. For all projects in the 2025 GAA contributing to food security, more than 60% of the allotted budget went to actions connected to “production and distribution systems,” which is largely dedicated to farm-to-market road projects. Assuming the allegations regarding corruption in flood control projects are true, these point to acts of greenwashing by some government agencies and officials. Misleading the public through claims of decisions supposedly being environment-friendly to mask corrupt practices does not just apply to the private sector. For the current administration, which has made climate action a priority agenda, this would cause even more damage to its reputation domestically and even at the global level. South Korea certainly has taken notice of the implications of these scandals. The way to trace which projects are aligned with national climate objectives is through the Climate Change Expenditure Tagging (CCET). Under this system, projects can be classified as contributing to adaptation or mitigation, and to the seven thematic areas under the country’s National Climate Change Action Plan (e.g., food security, water sufficiency, human security). It is intended to provide a transparent means of monitoring public funds spent on climate projects and inform decision-making. Instead, aside from the obvious imperative to purge corruption, the flood control scandals have exposed the weaknesses of the CCET system that need to be addressed if we want to avoid these incidents. Firstly, it is absurd to have so much of the national climate budget concentrated on only one agency. The executive and legislative branches must ensure a more even spread of public funds to address climate-relevant issues, including food security, water sufficiency, and sustainable energy through renewable energy. Secondly, there must be more support for strengthening monitoring and evaluation by the mandated agencies, the CCC and the Department of Budget and Management. Some of the billions of pesos from flood control projects can be reallotted to capacity-building for them to fulfill these tasks. Thirdly, there needs to be a stronger quality assurance for ensuring projects contribute to climate action. The current practice of agencies doing their own tagging needs to be reexamined and revised to ensure their proposed actions are justified as climate-tagged, not just for compliance or the appearance of one. Unknown to many people, there is a provision under the GAA itself that “all national government projects should be subjected to multi-scenario probabilistic analysis.” It is highly likely that some of the flood control projects did not comply to this, given what we have seen around us recently. There are actually a few bills currently filed in Congress that tries to address the CCET. For our collective sake, our lawmakers should seriously look into how to improve this system and amending that section of the GAA to turn “should” to “shall.” Any climate action without upholding justice at its core is nothing but a false solution. Canceling all flood control projects in 2026 is not the right move; communities remain just as prone to floods as they did before corruption started dominating headlines these days. It is another reminder to shift away from infrastructure-heavy funding and start taking care of our forests, rivers, and natural environment for the benefit of the Filipino people and not just to cater to business interests. Unless good governance becomes the norm in this country, the money stolen is given back, and everyone found guilty is punished instead of just leaving their posts, the hope arising from the peaceful demands of the people might also be too good to be true. 2028 is not that far away, though. – Rappler.com John Leo Algo is the national coordinator of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, the Philippines’ leading civil society coordination network on climate action. He is also the deputy executive director for programs and campaigns of Living Laudato Si’ Philippines. How does this make you feel?

text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. DANGER. The Pulangi River slowly eats away at the riverbank in Pagalungan, Maguindanao del Sur, eroding soil beneath a national highway and threatening its collapse. DPWH XII COTABATO CITY, Philippines – A vital stretch of highway in Maguindanao del Sur is on the brink of crumbling into the Pulangi River, a collapse that could sever one of key arteries in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The river, swollen and unruly after shifting its course, has chewed dangerously close to the Cotabato-Davao Highway. In Barangay Layog, Pagalungan town, just a sliver of earth now stands between the road and the encroaching current. Authorities have reduced traffic to a single lane, but this has created crippling congestion on a route that carries the lifeblood of trade and travel across the region. Local officials have sounded alarm bells, but their pleas come at a time when public trust in flood control programs is badly shaken. Across the country, scandals over padded contracts and ghost projects have hollowed out public confidence, casting doubt on whether urgent fixes in Maguindanao del Sur will arrive before the river takes the highway section itself. For some of them, the scandals explain why towns like Pagalungan – where a section of a national highway is several heavy rainfalls away from being swept into the Pulangi River – have been starved of funds for decades. “This situation is very alarming, and is in need of immediate action,” Maguindanao del Sur Representative Esmael “Toto” Mangudadatu said during an on-site inspection on Saturday, August 23, with former Pagalungan mayor and now Councilor Salik Mamasabulod. The Pulangi River, flowing from the mountains of Bukidnon and Cotabato, altered its course in recent years, displacing families and submerging farmlands. Its floodwaters are now gnawing at the national highway embankment, threatening to cut off a critical link between Cotabato and Davao. Mamasabulod noted that Pagalungan last received flood control funding in 1982, or 43 years ago, and estimated that at least 500 meters of embankment must be reinforced to protect the road and a nearby bridge. This brings the agency’s proposed budget down to P625.8 billion from the initial P881 billion. The DPWH also trimmed P3 billion worth of duplicate or completed projects, including overlapping road sections, rock netting, and cat’s eye and stud installations. In total, the agency’s proposed budget was slashed by P255 billion, or nearly 29%. The DPWH said Marcos recommended that the P255 billion freed up from the cut be used instead for programs in agriculture, education, healthcare, housing, labor, social welfare, and information technology. He linked the destruction of records to Magalong’s earlier report that the Baguio engineering office had been uncooperative with the ICI. The secretary added that he had tasked retired police general Arthur “Ato” Bisnar to investigate the incident. Bisnar, whom Dizon recommended for the post of DPWH undersecretary, has yet to receive his appointment papers. The ICI stressed that all records relating to public works are public property. Reyes urged DPWH officials to cooperate with the probe and preserve the integrity of all documents and evidence in their custody. Lacson said the panel has yet to open the files gathered by Hernandez due to a technical problem. “ Hindi pa namin na-unseal kasi nagkaroon ng kaunting glitch kasi naiwan ‘yung computer but sealed naman ‘yun ,” Lacson said. title: PANOORIN: Bilyon-bilyon ang pondo para sa flood control projects. Bakit baha pa rin?
text: MANILA, Philippines – Matagal nang problema ang baha sa Pilipinas. May mga proyekto ang gobyerno para maibsan ito. Magkano nga ba ang napupunta sa Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) para sa kanilang flood management programs? Panoorin ang report na ito ni Patrick Cruz. Delubyo na ang pondong ibinuhos ng gobyerno sa flood control projects. Ang napala natin? Delubyo rin. Bilyon-bilyon kada taon ang budget para sa flood control. Ngayong 2025, higit P248 billion ang nakuhang budget ng DPWH para sa flood control. Mula 2023 to 2025 sa ilalim ni President Ferdinand Marcos Jr .: P675 billion na ang total. Sa panahon ni president Rodrigo Duterte (2017–2022): P612.28 billion. Kay dating pangulong Noynoy Aquino (2011–2016): P181.7 billion. Sa loob ng nakalipas na 15 taon, umabot na sa P1.47 trillion ang nailaan ng gobyerno para lang sa flood management ng DPWH. Lahat ‘yan, pera ng bayan. Pera mo. Pera natin. Malalim at matagal nang problema ang baha sa Pilipinas. Kapag may baha, paralisado ang transportasyon , suspendido ang klase , apektado ang kabuhayan ng marami, maraming bahay ang lubog, at sa mga nakalipas na mga taon, daan-daan na ang namatay. Maraming dahilan ang pagbaha. ‘Andyan ang problema sa basura, poor urban planning, at climate change. Flood control sana ang isa sa mga solusyon. Bilyon-bilyon na ang nagastos sa flood control projects, pero tuwing umuulan, lubog pa rin ang Pilipinas. Ulan ba talaga ang problema o ang sistema? Ano sa tingin mo? Jire Carreon/Rappler MANILA, Philippines – New Speaker Bojie Dy said he wants the House to suspend its investigation into anomalous flood control projects and let the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) take the lead. “If it were only up to me, regarding infra comm, all reports and whatever happened in the infra comm should already be submitted to the ICI. title: [OPINION] Flood control issue brings PH to ‘tipping point’
text: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Why only now? After all, in July, a tropical cyclone whose local name starts with ‘C’ hit the Philippines and, with the southwest monsoon, brought massive flooding across the nation. This caused casualties and billions of pesos’ worth of damages to agriculture, livelihoods, and properties. It then led to widespread criticisms of flood control projects, which has a large share of the national budget, and calls for investigations. What was just mentioned is what actually happened last year, with “Carina.” And this happened again this year, with “Crising.” So why only now? Obviously, there have been public criticisms over failures like this before 2024 and 2025, but why is it only now that the outcry reached this level where it can no longer be ignored or overlooked? There are many factors that contributed to this. We can point to the President making accountability on mismanaged flood control projects a clear priority, as seen in his most recent State of the Nation Address (SONA). While a welcomed move only if there is a clear follow through, this is also political damage control regarding the administration’s public image that may not necessarily be reflected in public surveys. He did present the completion of over 5,500 flood control projects in last year’s SONA, which makes the current scandals even more harmful to how the public sees him and his administration. His candidates also had a relatively-underwhelming performance in the mid-term elections. We can also point to the public now having faces with whom to associate this form of corruption and incompetence. Among the ones drawing the most flak are influencers that also happen to be children of politicians and businesses, many of whom are directly linked to flood control projects. These so-called “nepo-babies” flaunting their luxury clothes, designer bags, and first-class trips on social media is not exactly a new development; they have been doing this for years. But contrasting their lavish lifestyles with the poverty, disasters, and other issues most of the nation are left to endure time and again has become an effective short-term way to make this issue relatable to ordinary Filipinos. We could look into these factors, among others, for reaching this point. Or it could be as simple as Filipinos simply having enough of wading through deep floods, cleaning their houses and streets, and losing income every single year — these days, it could now be every few months. Unfortunately, that last point can be interpreted as Filipinos once again only reacting to a problem when it directly affects them, no matter how long-running the issues are, when it has become more than just an occasional inconvenience. But better late than never, I guess. Some folks would call it a breaking point. But we will use “tipping point.” In scientific discourse, this is known as the moment when a series of small incidents over time cause a drastic and irreversible change in a system. In the context of the climate crisis, this would refer to continued global warming caused by pollution from human activities that cause widespread shifts in the likes of the water cycle and sea surface temperatures; both of these contribute to occurrences of extreme rainfall, formation of typhoons, and rising sea levels. But these days, it has never been clearer that this point would happen even faster through sheer impunity. And it has even more far-reaching effects than most people would realize. While flood control gets by far the most attention in the national climate discourse, as obviously important as this issue is, it is only one part of the national climate strategy. Unknown to most of the nation, many of the Philippines’ climate plans are being updated or developed in 2025. Many of these plans come with a condition — developed countries must provide finance and other means of support, largely because they are responsible for causing the climate crisis and aligned with the nation’s calls for climate justice to the global community. However, developed nations have failed to deliver not just to the Philippines, but other developing countries. For example, in the country’s current plan for reducing climate pollution, less than one percent of the estimated P4 trillion needed for its full implementation has been received about halfway through this decade. To make it worse, most of the support we end up getting from developed countries is in the form of loans. Translation: the public will end up paying this back, in one way or another. These billions of pesos wasted on these failed flood control projects could have been used to reduce the dependence on these loans and, subsequently, the country’s rising debt under the current government. They could have been used to prevent even more economic and non-economic losses and damages. That money could have been used for protecting our forests, helping our farmers, or actually mitigating floods. As much as the Philippine government rightfully echoes the call for accountability by global polluters, we must demand for accountability in our backyard. And this is where another way to look at the concept of ‘tipping point’ comes in. In the context of climate action, this would refer to people having a dramatic and more permanent shift in their behaviors and norms. In the current context, this would entail no longer simply treating disasters as an annual inconvenience, accountability as secondary to political patronage, and good governance as measured by popularity and immediate relief. We have the right to be skeptical. We have seen the reactions, the memes, and the outrage on social media before for a few months, before slowly going silent. We have seen previous pursuits of justice turned instead into a game of political machinations. But this time has to be different. The question is which of these tipping points the Philippines would reach first: the climate crisis, or climate action itself. The correct answer is the latter — and it must happen sooner than later. – Rappler.com A climate analyst, John Leo is the National Coordinator of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, the Philippines’ leading civil society network on climate action. He is also the Deputy Executive Director for Programs and Campaigns of Living Laudato Si’ Philippines. How does this make you feel?

Presidential Communications Office MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Wednesday, August 20, that his government is eyeing “economic sabotage” cases against contractors of big ghost flood control projects. Marcos made the statement in response to questions at a media interview in Purok 4, Barangay Piel in Baliuag, Bulacan, where he verified a citizen’s complaint about a non-existent — but fully paid for — P55-million reinforced concrete riverwall project Asked about the special fraud audit of the Commission on Audit on flood control projects in Bulacan, Marcos said the ghost project in Baliuag is an “example of falsification… because it was reported as completed.” “Kitang-kita naman na hindi completed. So, immediately that’s a falsification. So, that’s already a very big violation. And for the big ones, talagang I’m thinking very hard to — pipilahan natin sila ng economic sabotage,” he said. “ Tingnan natin, ha, ‘yung utang ng gobyerno ng Pilipinas, ng Republika, ay mababawasan kung naging maayos lahat itong pag-ano. Kasi ngayon babalikan na natin ngayon ito, saan napunta ‘yung pera? Hahabulin natin, kakasuhan natin sila. How long will that take? Hindi ba? ” he added. (It’s evident that it’s not complete. So immediately, that’s falsification. So, that’s already a very big violation. And for the big ones, I’m really thinking very hard to line up economic sabotage [cases against them]. Just look, the Philippine government’s debts would be reduced if these projects were done well. Because now, we have to go back to them — where did the money go to? We will run after them, file cases against them. How long will it take? Right?) In a Facebook post later that day, Marcos announced that he had ordered the blacklisting of SYMS Construction Trading, and also said that it will be charged for violation of Republic Act 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and malversation of public funds through falsification of public documents. “Ang SYMS Construction Trading ay agad na iba-blacklist at haharap sa mga kaso sa ilalim ng Revised Penal Code at RA 3019. Hahanapin at sisiyasatin pa natin ang iba pa nilang proyekto. Hindi natin palalampasin ito. Sususpendihin at kakasuhan ang lahat ng opisyal na nag-authorize at nakipagsabwatan dito,” Marcos said. (SYMS Construction Trading has been immediately blacklisted and will face charges under the Revised Penal Code and RA 3019. We will scrutinize their other projects. We will not let this pass. We will suspend and file cases against officials who authorized [the projects] and connived with them.) Marcos told the media in Baliuag that he went to Barangay Piel, acting on a report his office received through his “citizens’ complaint Sumbong sa Pangulo” website. Upon inspection, he saw no progress or activity for the 220-meter project that cost the government  P55,730,911.60. As of June, Marcos said, the report stated that it was “100% complete and also fully paid.” The Presidential Communications Office posted the official receipts of the payment of the Department of Public Works and Highways Bulacan 1st District Engineering Office to Malolos-based SYMS Construction Trading: the first payment of P43,492,098 on March 19, 2025, and P5,948,792.98 on June 30, 2025. “Wala kaming makita na kahit isang… hollow block, isang ano ng semento, walang equipment dito. Lahat itong project na ito ghost project. Walang ginawa na trabaho dito,” he told the media. (We didn’t see even a single… hollow block, any cement, no equipment here. This is a ghost project. No work was done here.) “I’m not disappointed. I’m angry,” he also said. Marcos said there was an ongoing flood control project on the other side of the riverbank, and that the two contractors involved were “pointing fingers” at each other, explaining that the riverwall project could not begin until the other project was finished. Adding to the mystery, he said, was the difficulty in locating the contract for the project. Marcos suspects that the record was “lost” as the project was repeatedly subcontracted, and the chief district engineer had been replaced over the years. The ones in charge are looking for the records, he said. “Since we put up the website, ang dami talagang sumusulat (many people have messaged us) and this a perfect example of the abuse that is being done by some of these contractors,” Marcos said. “Ongoing naman ‘yung ating mga investigation. Pinag-aaralan namin lahat. Tinitingnan namin lahat ng mga sinusumbong sa amin. And we will not stop. We will keep going until ma-identify na mabuti at makasuhan nang mabuti lahat itong mga contractor at kung sinoman ang mga nakakuha ng kontrata,” he added. (All of the investigations are ongoing. We are studying all of this. We are checking all of the complaints we receive. And we will not stop. We will keep going until all these contractors and anyone else who got contracts are identified and sued.) Marcos said the modus of some contractors is to secure the government contract, and then “sell” the contract to a subcontractor. “Bahala na kung ‘yung subcontractor kung itutuloy niya ‘yung project. Bahala na sila kung maganda, kung sub – kung nasa standard o substandard kaya napapabayaan. At ‘yung iba, hindi na lang itinutuloy.… Anyway, we will keep going. Hahabulin natin silang lahat,” the President said. (The subcontractor will decide if they will continue the project. It would be up to them if [the project] is standard or substandard, that’s why it gets neglected. And there are those who just don’t continue [the project]. Anyway, we will keep going. We will run after all of them.) Marcos earlier bared a list of the top 15 contractors of flood control projects in the country, based on the initial findings of an audit he had ordered during his recent State of the Nation Address (SONA). Of these firms, six received ratings of “unsatisfactory” or “poor” in previous years . The Senate blue ribbon committee has begun probing anomalous flood control projects. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?
